query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Upon moderate heat treatment, the initially metastable Mg-rich solid solution in a lightweight HEA transitions toward more stable intermetallic phases, which locally redistribute Mg and other passivating elements in the microstructure, thereby enhancing the protective oxide layer formation and slowing corrosion and high-temperature oxidation compared to the as-cast alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a partially supersaturated solid solution and minor intermetallics, overall density <6 g/cm3.
generation.intervention: In-situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy during controlled annealing (e.g., 200–500 °C), with concurrent electrochemical and thermogravimetric monitoring.
generation.conditions: Heating under inert atmosphere followed by exposure to a corrosive medium and high-temperature oxidizing environment.
generation.structural_mediator: Nucleation and growth of stable or partially stable intermetallic phases from the Mg-enriched solid solution, altering local chemistry and passivation film composition.
generation.mechanism: As Mg-rich domains transform, other passivating elements (e.g., Ti, Al, or Zn) concentrate in the newly formed intermetallics and surrounding matrix, modifying surface film chemistry and improving oxide adherence. This hinders oxide spallation and reduces micro-galvanic coupling, thereby lowering corrosion and oxidation rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial as-cast state, the alloy will exhibit a lower corrosion rate and improved oxidation resistance due to more protective surface films, with notably slower oxidation kinetics at elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: Higher corrosion current densities and accelerated oxide scale breakdown in the as-cast, supersaturated state.
generation.boundary: Effects are most pronounced at moderate heat treatment temperatures (≤500 °C). Rapid heating or exposure at higher temperatures may bypass or alter the intermediate transformation stages, limiting the validity of the mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: Exact phase fractions and element partitioning, and their quantitative impact on passivation and oxidation kinetics, remain insufficiently characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy sets: one kept strictly in the as-cast metastable condition, the other subjected to stepwise annealing (200–500 °C). Track phase evolution in real time via in-situ XRD/SEM during the thermal cycle, then compare corrosion and oxidation performance.
measurements: Monitoring of newly formed intermetallic phases by high-temperature XRD peak intensities over time
Electron microscopy to quantify changes in local composition
Electrochemical tests (e.g. potentiodynamic polarization) pre- and post-annealing
Mass-change measurements of samples after isothermal oxidation at elevated temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If in-situ characterization and subsequent environmental tests reveal negligible intermetallic formation or no improvement/deterioration in corrosion or oxidation resistance compared to the as-cast alloy, the proposed mechanism is not supported.

cited_evidence.text: This study investigated the effects of composition and processing on the microstructure, hardness, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance of spark plasma sintered Mg-Ti-Zn alloys. Key findings include: MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn alloys were produced via ball milling and spark plasma sintering. XRD, SEM, and STEM analyses revealed the presence of multiple phases. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high hardness and stiffness, which were much higher than those of any commercial Mg alloy. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high corrosion resistance (indicated by the high corrosion potential and low corrosion current density) and passivation, which were attributed to the formation of a Ti rich surface film. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining mechanical alloying and SPS to engineer Mg-containing multi-principal element alloys with a rare combination of high hardness and corrosion resistance. This strategy offers a new pathway for designing lightweight structural or biomedical materials that overcome the traditional strength–corrosion trade-off in Mg and Zn alloys. AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) of the Cantor type (CoCrFeMnNi) are widely recognized as model systems for studying the relationships between composition, microstructure, and functional performance. In this study, atomized Cantor alloy powders were consolidated using spark plasma sintering (SPS) under systematically varied process parameters (temperature and dwell time). The densification behavior, microstructural evolution, and mechanical response were investigated using Archimedes’ density measurements, Vickers hardness testing, compression tests, scanning electron microscopy, and EDS mapping. The results reveal a non-linear relationship between sintering temperature and densification, with maximum relative densities obtained at 1050 °C and 1100 °C for short dwell times. Despite the ultrafast nature of SPS, grain growth was observed, particularly at elevated temperatures and extended dwell times, challenging the assumption that SPS inherently limits grain coarsening. All sintered samples retained a single-phase FCC structure with homogeneous elemental distribution, and no phase segregation or secondary precipitates were detected. The alloys JZ1 and JZ2 had lower Ge and Sn concentrations and the same but lower Ti concentrations than the alloys studied by Vellios and Tsakiropoulos (see []) and Li and Tsakiropoulos [] and references within and did not suffer from complete disintegration to powders, instead their scales spalled off and scale fragments disintegrated into powder. This suggests (i) that the simultaneous presence of Ge and Sn in the alloys “controlled and improved” the effect of Ge and (ii) that the synergy of these two elements with Hf, Ta, Ti, and W was also beneficial regarding control of pest oxidation. The oxidation resistance of the alloy JZ2 at 800 °C was slightly improved, most likely because of its lower vol.% of the Nbss and higher Sn+Ge content, compared with the alloy JZ1. The results of this work and the literature suggest that additional research should aim to find out whether the oxidation of Nb-silicide-based alloys with Ta and W additions in the pest regime could be improved with simultaneous addition of Sn and Ge with Al and Cr.

decision.trend: Initial Al–Mg-rich lightweight complex concentrated alloys were induction melted and recognized for multiple intermetallic phases but left open the exact transformation pathways. Later work on Mg-containing systems (e.g., MgTiZn, Mg4TiZn) linked grain-boundary or matrix precipitates to corrosion improvement, yet the step-by-step evolution from metastable to stable phases remained unclear. These studies achieved modest success in correlating microstructures with properties but did not fully resolve how non-equilibrium Mg-based phases transform at high temperature or under corrosive conditions, nor how those transformations impact oxidation resistance.
decision.unsolved: It remains unknown precisely how and when metastable Mg-containing phases give way to stable intermetallics, how those transitions alter passive film chemistry, and whether they promote or impede surface-protective oxide formation during corrosive or high-temperature exposure.
decision.lever: Perform in-situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy on as-cast metastable Mg-containing HEAs during controlled annealing steps (e.g., 200–500 °C). Concurrent electrochemical and thermogravimetric measurements map real-time changes in surface films and oxidation kinetics, allowing direct observation of how newly formed intermetallics alter local chemistry and passivation layers relative to the initial metastable microstructure.
decision.why: Prior work has shown Mg’s strong influence on phase stability and corrosion behavior, but has not traced the dynamic microstructural changes that control passivation and oxide formation over time. Direct in-situ tracking addresses the persistent gap in understanding the transformation pathways and how they govern environmental resistance.
